narrative:
You learned the road does not ask who your parents were. It asks who keeps walking after the fire goes out, after the last innkeeper says no, after a friend takes the easier path without you.

You still carry a button from the coat of Osric, who taught you that lesson. The metal has been rubbed smooth by bad weather and worse nights. You have never decided whether keeping it is loyalty or cowardice.

At the edge of another nameless village, a yellowed field catches your eye. You know the look of a place beginning to run out of chances - but that is tomorrow's problem. Tonight there is only the road, and the button, and the old habit of deciding, again, what to do with both.

You keep walking at your own pace. He glances back once, mid-stride, and something in his face flickers - not hurt exactly, more like a bet he'd made with himself and just lost.

He doesn't slow down to argue about it. By the time you reach the well yourself, he's long gone.

narrative:
The village comes into view past a rise in the road, and with it the field you noticed from a distance - worse up close. Whole rows of what should be waist-high by now barely clear your ankle, yellowed at the tip like something's been drinking the color out of them from the inside.

A farmer stands at the field's edge, not working it, just looking at it the way you look at a wound you're not ready to touch yet.

narrative:
It's not blight, not exactly - the soil's gone thin and starved, over-planted one season too many by people with no season to spare for letting it rest. You could tell the farmer that. You're not sure it would help him do anything differently, given what's coming either way.

He notices you crouched over his ruined rows and doesn't ask what you found. Just nods once, like confirming something he already suspected and didn't want confirmed.

You crouch, dig your fingers into the dirt, and come away with nothing more useful than dirty hands and a farmer watching you with the particular patience of someone who's seen a dozen strangers do exactly this and offer exactly nothing afterward.

@Farmer: You're not the first to poke at it. Won't be the last, either. Dirt keeps its own counsel.

narrative:
The treeline the travelers mentioned narrows the road ahead into something a person could block without much effort. Sure enough, a figure steps out - dressed too well for a bandit, speaking too formally to be anything else.

@Tollkeeper: You are, I regret to inform you, standing upon a toll road. Passage is ten silver. Refusal is also an option, of course. Every option is an option, until it isn't.

narrativeVariants.origin.royal == true:
The treeline the travelers mentioned narrows the road ahead into something a person could block without much effort. Sure enough, a figure steps out - and something in his expression shifts the moment he sees your bearing, recognition curdling into something colder.

@Tollkeeper: House Aldric. Of course. I once collected taxes in your father's name, you know, before your father's court decided my methods were beneath the crown's dignity. How amusing, to collect from you instead now. Passage is ten silver. Or something more interesting than silver, given who you are.

narrative:
One of the travelers goes quiet for a moment before answering, the way people do when a story used to be sacred and isn't anymore.

@Traveler: Used to be you could see its towers from three villages over. Then one hero or another - stories don't agree which, don't agree why - burned it to the ground. Nobody agrees on that either: was it wrath, or was it mercy, put to the wrong use. My grandmother wouldn't say the hero's name out loud. Said naming it gave it more power than it already had.

narrative:
@Traveler: Officially? Died peacefully, passed the crown to House Aldric's founder, everyone wept, very tidy. Unofficially, my grandfather's grandfather used to say the old king simply stopped being convenient to keep around, and House Aldric was very convenient indeed at exactly the right moment.

Saoirse doesn't confirm or deny it. She just watches you take the story in, like she's testing which parts you believe.

Whether it's a dragon like the old stories or something that just wants people to think it's a dragon - that part, nobody's gotten close enough to confirm.
